questions.question: What does 'Scale Out' mean in the context of AWS EBS storage?

options.text: Increasing the size of an existing EBS volume
Adding a new, separate EBS volume alongside the existing one
Moving the EBS volume to a different Availability Zone
Converting a GP2 volume to GP3

explanation.correct: Scale Out means adding extra resources — in this case, attaching a new EBS volume to the EC2 instance to use in parallel with the existing one.
explanation.why: A is Scale Up. C is not possible without a snapshot. D is a volume modification, not scaling.

questions.question: Which EBS volume type allows you to independently configure IOPS and throughput without changing the storage size?

explanation.correct: GP3 allows independent configuration of IOPS (up to 16,000) and throughput (up to 1,000 MiB/s) separately from storage capacity.
explanation.why: GP2 ties IOPS to storage size (3 IOPS/GB). st1 and sc1 are HDD types and don't support configurable IOPS in the same way.

questions.question: What command lists all block devices attached to a Linux system?

explanation.correct: lsblk (list block devices) shows all attached disks, their sizes, partitions, and where they are mounted.
explanation.why: df -h shows file system usage. blkid shows UUIDs. fdisk -l shows partition tables — but lsblk is the most common command for a quick overview.

questions.question: What does the mkfs command do?

options.text: Mounts a disk to a directory
Lists all file systems on the system
Creates (formats) a file system on a disk

explanation.correct: mkfs (Make File System) formats a raw disk device and creates a file system structure (like XFS or EXT4) so the OS can read and write to it.
explanation.why: Mounting is done with the mount command. Listing file systems uses df or lsblk. Disk checks use fsck.

questions.question: After attaching a new EBS volume and mounting it temporarily, what happens after an EC2 reboot?

options.text: The mount point is lost — the OS forgets the mount

explanation.correct: The mount command creates a temporary mount for the current session only. After a reboot, Linux reads /etc/fstab to know what to mount. If the volume isn't listed there, it won't be mounted.
explanation.why: The volume stays attached to EC2 (B is wrong). The volume is not deleted (D is wrong). A is wrong — temporary mounts don't persist.

questions.question: What file must you edit to make an EBS mount permanent across reboots?

explanation.correct: /etc/fstab (file system table) is the configuration file Linux reads at boot to automatically mount file systems. Adding your EBS volume entry here makes it mount permanently.
explanation.why: /etc/hosts maps hostnames to IPs. /etc/mtab and /proc/mounts show currently mounted file systems but are managed by the OS, not manually edited.

questions.question: Why should you use UUID instead of device name (e.g., /dev/nvme1n1) in /etc/fstab?

options.text: Device names are case-sensitive but UUIDs are not
Device names can change after reboot; UUIDs are permanent identifiers for the disk
UUIDs are shorter and easier to type
Only UUIDs are supported in newer Linux versions

explanation.correct: Device names like nvme1n1 can change if disks are reattached in different orders. UUIDs are unique permanent identifiers assigned to each file system, so they reliably identify the same disk regardless of device name.
explanation.why: A, C, and D are all incorrect. The real reason is reliability and persistence of identification.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'nofail' option in an /etc/fstab entry?

options.text: Tells Linux to check the disk for errors on every boot
Prevents the system from failing to boot if the disk is unavailable
Disables journaling on the file system

explanation.correct: nofail tells Linux to continue booting even if this particular disk is unavailable or cannot be mounted. Without nofail, a missing disk can cause EC2 to get stuck in a boot loop.
explanation.why: Disk checks use the last column (pass number) in fstab. Read-only uses 'ro' option. Journaling is a file system setting, not an fstab option.

questions.question: What type of backup is an EBS Snapshot?

explanation.correct: EBS Snapshots are incremental — the first snapshot stores all used data, but subsequent snapshots only store blocks that have changed since the last snapshot. This saves storage space and cost.
explanation.why: Full backups copy everything every time. Differential backups copy changes since the last full backup. EBS snapshots specifically use an incremental approach.

questions.question: Where are EBS Snapshots stored?

explanation.correct: EBS Snapshots are stored automatically in Amazon S3, but in an AWS-managed bucket that you cannot see or directly access in your S3 console.
explanation.why: Storing on the volume itself would defeat the backup purpose. Glacier is for archival. Instance store is ephemeral local storage. Snapshots go to S3.

questions.question: You have an 8GB EBS volume with only 1.6GB of data on it. How large will the first snapshot approximately be?

explanation.correct: EBS Snapshots capture the used data on the volume, not the total allocated size. If 1.6GB is used on an 8GB volume, the first snapshot is approximately 1.6GB.
explanation.why: You are charged for data stored in the snapshot, not the full volume size. This is a common exam misconception.

questions.question: Which EBS volume types CANNOT be used as EC2 boot (root) volumes?

explanation.correct: HDD volume types (st1 — Throughput Optimized, and sc1 — Cold HDD) cannot be used as boot volumes. Only SSD types (GP2, GP3, io1, io2) can boot an EC2 instance.
explanation.why: All SSD types support boot volumes. HDD types are optimized for sequential throughput, not the random I/O patterns required during system boot.

questions.question: An EC2 instance is in Availability Zone ap-south-1b. You need to attach a new EBS volume to it. In which AZ must you create the volume?

explanation.correct: EBS volumes are AZ-specific resources. A volume can only be attached to EC2 instances within the same Availability Zone. You must create the volume in ap-south-1b to attach it to an instance in that AZ.
explanation.why: EBS volumes cannot span AZs. To use a volume in a different AZ, you must create a snapshot and then create a new volume from the snapshot in the desired AZ.

questions.question: You want to move an EBS volume from us-east-1 to ap-south-1. What is the correct process?

options.text: Detach the volume and reattach it in ap-south-1
Create a snapshot → Copy snapshot to ap-south-1 → Create volume from snapshot in ap-south-1
Use the EBS Transfer service to move volumes between regions
Modify the volume's region attribute in the console

explanation.correct: EBS volumes cannot be directly moved between regions. The process is: create a snapshot of the volume → copy the snapshot to the target region → create a new volume from the snapshot in the target region.
explanation.why: Volumes are region/AZ-bound. There is no direct transfer service. Region attributes cannot be changed on an existing volume.

questions.question: You take a snapshot of an EBS volume while the EC2 is still running and writing data. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The snapshot will be corrupt and unusable
AWS automatically pauses the instance during snapshot
The snapshot is crash-consistent — it captures a moment in time, which may leave some application data in an unwritten state
Running instances cannot have snapshots taken

explanation.correct: Snapshots of running instances are crash-consistent — like pulling a power plug. The OS data is captured at a point in time, but application buffers that hadn't been flushed to disk may be missing. For application-consistent snapshots, pause writes or use VSS (Windows) / fsfreeze (Linux) before snapshotting.
explanation.why: Snapshots aren't corrupt (A), AWS doesn't pause the instance (B), and you can absolutely snapshot running instances (D).

questions.question: What command retrieves the UUID of a block device?

explanation.correct: The blkid command (block ID) retrieves the UUID and file system type of a block device. You need this UUID to add a permanent entry in /etc/fstab.
explanation.why: lsblk shows device structure but not UUIDs. df shows usage. fdisk is for partition management.

questions.question: After restoring an XFS-formatted EBS snapshot to a new EC2 instance, you get a UUID conflict error when mounting. What is the correct mount command?

explanation.correct: The -o nouuid option tells the XFS driver to ignore the UUID conflict and mount the volume anyway. This is needed when restoring a snapshot to a different instance because the volume inherits the original XFS UUID.
explanation.why: A will fail with the UUID conflict. C would format the disk, erasing all data. -f (force) is not the correct flag for this issue.

questions.question: You create a snapshot of a volume on Monday (Snapshot 1). On Wednesday, you add 500MB of files. On Friday, you take another snapshot (Snapshot 2). How does AWS store Snapshot 2?

options.text: Stores a full copy of the entire volume again
Stores only the 500MB of new/changed data added since Snapshot 1
Stores the difference between Monday and Friday as a single full backup

explanation.correct: EBS Snapshots are incremental. Snapshot 2 only stores the 500MB of blocks that changed between Snapshot 1 and Snapshot 2. AWS references Snapshot 1 for unchanged data.
explanation.why: No full copy is made (A is wrong). Snapshot 1 is not replaced (C). The term 'differential' (D) is different from incremental — snapshots are incremental.

questions.question: What is the command to mount all file systems listed in /etc/fstab?

explanation.correct: sudo mount -a (mount all) reads /etc/fstab and mounts all listed file systems that aren't already mounted. Use this to test a new fstab entry without rebooting.
explanation.why: mount /all and mountall are not valid standard commands. fstab --apply does not exist.

questions.question: Which service can automate the creation and deletion of EBS Snapshots on a schedule?

explanation.correct: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) automates snapshot creation, retention, and deletion based on policies you define. AWS Backup is also correct but DLM is the most direct service specifically for EBS snapshot lifecycle management.
explanation.why: CloudWatch Events can trigger Lambda but isn't a native snapshot scheduler. CloudFormation is for infrastructure provisioning, not backup scheduling.

questions.question: You need to restore an EBS snapshot but the target EC2 is in a different region than where the snapshot was taken. What must you do first?

options.text: Create a volume from the snapshot — cross-region volumes are supported
Copy the snapshot to the target region first, then create a volume from the copy
Use AWS Direct Connect to transfer the snapshot
Convert the snapshot to an AMI, then copy the AMI

explanation.correct: Snapshots are region-scoped. To use a snapshot in a different region, you must copy it to the target region (Actions → Copy Snapshot in console, or aws ec2 copy-snapshot in CLI). Then create a volume from the copy in the target region.
explanation.why: Cross-region volumes from a local snapshot is not possible. Direct Connect is for network connectivity. Converting to AMI is unnecessary extra steps (though AMIs can also be copied cross-region).

questions.question: An application requires extremely low latency I/O (< 1ms) and high throughput for a relational database. Which EBS volume type is most appropriate?

options.text: io2 Block Express — Provisioned IOPS SSD

explanation.correct: io2 Block Express offers the highest IOPS (up to 256,000), sub-millisecond latency, and 99.999% durability. It's designed specifically for I/O-intensive databases like Oracle, SAP HANA, and high-performance MySQL.
explanation.why: GP3 is great for general workloads but not optimized for extreme IOPS. st1 is HDD and has much higher latency. sc1 is the coldest/cheapest HDD and not suitable for databases.

questions.question: You delete a snapshot that was used to create an EBS volume. What happens to that volume?

options.text: The volume is unaffected — it continues to function normally
The volume loses data that wasn't in the latest snapshot

explanation.correct: Once a volume is created from a snapshot, it becomes fully independent. Deleting the source snapshot does not affect any volumes or AMIs created from it. The volume has its own complete copy of the data.
explanation.why: Snapshots and volumes are independent once the volume is created. There is no ongoing dependency after volume creation.

questions.question: Your company policy requires all EBS snapshots to be encrypted at rest. You already have an unencrypted snapshot. How do you create an encrypted version?

options.text: Edit the existing snapshot and enable encryption
Copy the snapshot and enable encryption during the copy operation
Encryption can only be enabled when creating the original snapshot
Use KMS to automatically encrypt all existing snapshots retroactively

explanation.correct: You cannot encrypt an existing unencrypted snapshot in-place. However, when you copy a snapshot (Actions → Copy Snapshot), you can enable encryption during the copy process. The copy will be encrypted; the original remains unencrypted.
explanation.why: Snapshots are immutable once created — you cannot modify their encryption status. KMS doesn't retroactively encrypt existing snapshots. Creating a new encrypted copy is the standard approach.

questions.question: What is the relationship between EBS Snapshots and AMIs?

options.text: AMIs and Snapshots are identical — different names for the same thing
An AMI includes one or more snapshots plus boot configuration (block device mappings, kernel settings)
Snapshots include AMIs plus additional storage metadata
AMIs are created independently of snapshots

explanation.correct: An AMI is built on top of snapshots. It includes one or more EBS snapshots (for the root and additional volumes) PLUS launch configuration like the kernel ID, architecture, and block device mappings. A snapshot alone is just data; an AMI is a launchable template.
explanation.why: They are not identical (A). Snapshots don't contain AMIs (C). Creating an AMI always creates underlying snapshots (D is wrong).

questions.question: A user runs 'sudo mount /dev/nvme1n1 /data' and gets 'mount: wrong filesystem type, missing code page or helper program'. What is most likely wrong?

options.text: The disk has not been formatted yet — no file system exists on it

explanation.correct: This error typically means the OS cannot determine the file system type because none has been created. A fresh EBS volume has no file system — you must format it first with mkfs before mounting.
explanation.why: A would give a 'device not found' error. C would give 'mount point does not exist'. D would give a permission denied error. The wrong filesystem type error points to an unformatted disk.

questions.question: What happens to EBS snapshots when you delete the originating EBS volume?

options.text: All snapshots of that volume are automatically deleted
Snapshots are preserved independently in S3 — they are not deleted
Snapshots become read-only and cannot be used to create new volumes
The most recent snapshot is kept; older ones are deleted

explanation.correct: EBS Snapshots are independent of the source volume. Deleting a volume does NOT delete its snapshots. The snapshots continue to exist in S3 and can still be used to create new volumes.
explanation.why: Snapshots are independent objects you must delete manually. They are fully usable after the source volume is gone.

questions.question: You want to share an EBS snapshot with another AWS account. Which statement is correct?

options.text: EBS snapshots cannot be shared — you must create an AMI first
You can make a snapshot public or share it with specific AWS account IDs
Sharing is only possible within the same AWS Organization
Encrypted snapshots cannot be shared under any circumstances

explanation.correct: EBS Snapshots can be shared: you can make them public (any AWS account can create volumes from them) or share with specific account IDs. Encrypted snapshots can also be shared if you share the KMS key with the recipient account.
explanation.why: Snapshots can be shared directly without needing an AMI. Sharing works across organizations. Encrypted snapshots can be shared with KMS key sharing.

questions.question: How does EBS pricing for snapshots work when taking multiple snapshots of the same volume over time?

options.text: You pay for the full volume size for every snapshot
You pay for the total used data on the first snapshot, plus only the changed blocks for each subsequent snapshot
All snapshots after the first are free
You pay a flat monthly fee per snapshot regardless of size

explanation.correct: The first snapshot captures all used data (e.g., 1.6GB on an 8GB volume). Each subsequent snapshot only stores the blocks that changed. You pay per GB stored across all your snapshots in the region.
explanation.why: You never pay for the full volume size — only used/changed data. Subsequent snapshots are not free. There is no flat fee; pricing is per GB stored.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the difference between GP2 and GP3 in terms of IOPS scaling?

options.text: GP2 provides more IOPS than GP3 at all storage sizes
GP2 IOPS scale automatically with volume size (3 IOPS/GB, max 16,000); GP3 provides a baseline 3,000 IOPS regardless of size, configurable up to 16,000
Both GP2 and GP3 require manual IOPS configuration
GP3 IOPS scale with volume size just like GP2

explanation.correct: GP2 automatically gives 3 IOPS per GB (so a 100GB GP2 volume gets 300 IOPS). GP3 gives a flat baseline of 3,000 IOPS for any size volume, and you can configure up to 16,000 IOPS independently of storage size. GP3 is generally more cost-effective.
explanation.why: GP3 is not always more IOPS than GP2 at large sizes — they have the same max. GP3 doesn't require IOPS config (baseline is automatic). GP3 doesn't scale with size.
